rationale: B wins because it turns Replit's weakest disclosed hole into actual story machinery. A's "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat" is respectable, but B's "Replit charges by usage for an agent it won't say how often gets the app right" has sharper conflict, cleaner stakes, and a billing question a reporter would actually ask. The benchmark angle, "Here is how many ran without a fix," is not padding; it is the missing method.
gaps_in_A: "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat" overstates the pricing fact. The update says usage-based pricing sits on top of subscriptions, not that seats are being replaced by work units.
A buries the best reliability story inside proof and questions: "how often generated apps work without fixes" should have become a reporter-testable benchmark or pricing-risk angle.
"Replit built its name teaching people to code" is a nice line, but the update only says Replit is used heavily in education. History-of-the-company framing needs backup.
The education angle misses the operational question B catches: whether the agent is enabled on education accounts and whether instructors can disable it.
gaps_in_B: "tens of millions of hobbyists" is invented. The update says tens of millions of users and positioning for non-engineers/vibe coders, not hobbyists.

"the same product will land in the accounts schools already use" assumes education-account availability the update does not provide. B knows this is a hole because it later asks whether the agent is enabled on education accounts.
"Replit's bet: tens of millions of hobbyists would rather describe an app than code one" conflates total claimed users with the target buyer segment before asking for the breakdown.
"Story type: defensive-comment" is a weird label for a pricing/business-model story. The angle itself works, but the taxonomy is wearing the wrong suit.
